butir.teks: And it was said: when the teacher combines three things, the blessing is completed through them for the learner: patience, humility, and good character. And when the learner combines three things, the blessing is completed through them for the teacher: intellect, proper conduct (adab), and good understanding.
In sum, the character traits that the Qur'an brought are never lacking in the scholars of the Hereafter, because they learn the Qur'an in order to act upon it, not for leadership.

Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) said, "We lived through a period of time in which one of us was given faith before the Qur'an, and a surah would be revealed and he would learn its lawful and forbidden matters, its commands and prohibitions, and the place where he ought to stop in it. And I have seen men, one of whom is given the Qur'an before faith, and he recites from the Opening of the Book to its end, not knowing what it commands, what it prohibits, or the place where he ought to stop in it; he scatters it as one scatters poor dates (daqal) (٣)." And in another report with a similar meaning: "We, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him),

were given faith before the Qur'an, and after you there will come a people who are given the Qur'an before faith. They uphold its letters and neglect its limits and its rights. They say, 'We have recited, so who recites better than we do; we have taught, so who knows more than we do.' That is their portion (١).
And in one wording: "Those are the worst of this community."

And it was said: five traits of character are among the signs of the scholars of the Hereafter, understood from five verses of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: reverential fear (khashya), humility in prayer (khushu'), humility, good character, and preferring the Hereafter over this world, which is renunciation (zuhd). As for reverential fear, it is from His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 35:28⟧. As for humility in prayer, it is from His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 3:199⟧. As for humility, it is from His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 15:88⟧. As for good character, it is from His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 3:159⟧. As for renunciation, it is from His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 28:80⟧. And when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) recited His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 6:125⟧, he was asked, "What is this expansion?" He said, "When light is cast into the heart, the chest is expanded and opened wide for it." It was asked, "Is there a sign of that?" He (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Yes: distancing oneself from the abode of delusion, turning back to the abode of eternity, and preparing for death before it descends (٢)." And among them is that most of his inquiry be into the knowledge of deeds and into what corrupts them, disturbs hearts, stirs up whispering, and raises evil, for the root of religion is guarding against evil, and therefore it was said
I knew evil, not for the sake of evil, but in order to guard against it ...
And whoever among people does not know evil falls into it ...

Because practical deeds are close at hand, and their furthest limit, indeed their highest, is persevering in the remembrance of Allah Most High with the heart and the tongue. The real matter lies in knowing what corrupts and disturbs them. This is among the things whose branches are many and whose ramifications are long, and all of it is among the things for which the need is most often pressing and which afflict everyone who travels the path of the Hereafter. As for the scholars of this world, they pursue rare ramifications in judgments and rulings, and toil in devising cases that ages pass without ever occurring; and if they do occur, they occur for others, not for them, and when they occur, there are many to handle them. And they leave what is inseparable from them and recurs for them in the hours of the night and the ends of the day, in their passing thoughts, their whisperings, and their deeds. How far from happiness is the one who sold his own pressing concern for another's rare concern, preferring nearness to creation and acceptance by them over drawing near to Allah, glorified is He.

And it was said to Hudhayfa, "We see you speaking words that are not heard from anyone else among the Companions; from where did you take them?" He said, "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) singled me out for it. People used to ask him about good, and I used to ask him about evil, fearing that I would fall into it, and I knew that knowledge of good would not get ahead of me (٣)." And once he said, "So I knew that whoever"
does not know evil does not know good

And in another wording: "They used to say, 'O Messenger of Allah, what is there for one who does such and such?' asking him about the merits of deeds, and I used to say, 'O Messenger of Allah, what spoils such and such?' When he saw me asking about the blights of deeds, he singled me out for this knowledge."

Hudhayfa (may Allah be pleased with him) was also singled out for knowledge of the hypocrites, and was set apart in knowing the knowledge of hypocrisy, its causes, and the subtleties of trials. Umar, Uthman, and the senior Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) used to ask him about trials, general and particular. He used to be asked about the hypocrites, and he would tell the number of those who remained of them but would not tell their names. And Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to ask him about himself, whether he knew in him anything of hypocrisy, and he cleared him of that. And when Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was invited to a funeral to pray over it, he would look: if Hudhayfa was present, he prayed over it, and if not, he left it. And Hudhayfa was called the keeper of the secret.

So attention to the stations (maqamat) and states (ahwal) of the heart is the habit of the scholars of the Hereafter, because the heart is what strives toward nearness to Allah Most High. This branch has become strange and effaced, and when a scholar takes up anything of it, it is thought strange and far-fetched, and it is said, "This is the embellishment of the preachers; where is real verification?" And they consider that verification lies in the subtleties of disputations. And truly he spoke the truth who said
The ways are many, while the way of truth is single ... and those who travel the way of truth are lone individuals
They are not recognised, and their aims are not perceived ... for they walk unhurried, in moderation
And people are heedless of what is intended for them ... and most of them are asleep, away from the path of truth

In sum, most people incline only to what is easier and more suited to their natures, for the truth is bitter, standing upon it is hard, grasping it is severe, and its path is rugged, especially knowing the traits of the heart and purifying it of blameworthy character, for that is a constant pulling out of the spirit. Whoever pursues it stands in the position of one who drinks medicine, enduring its bitterness in hope of recovery, and stands in the position of one who has made the span of his life his fast, so he endures hardships in order that his breaking of the fast be at death. And how could desire for this path ever be abundant? Therefore it was said that in Basra there were one hundred and twenty who spoke in preaching and admonition, and there was none who spoke on the knowledge of certainty, the states of hearts, and the traits of the inner except three of them: Sahl at-Tustari, as-Subayhi, and Abd ar-Rahim. A countless great crowd used to sit with those, and with these a small number, seldom exceeding ten, because the precious and rare is fit only for the elite, while what is given to everyone, its matter is light.

And among them is that his reliance in his knowledge be on his insight and his perception through the purity of his heart, not on pages and books, nor on imitation (taqlid) of what he hears from others. The only one imitated is the Lawgiver (peace and blessings be upon him) in what he commanded and said, and the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) are imitated only insofar as their action indicates that they heard it from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him).

Then, when he imitates the Lawgiver (peace and blessings be upon him) in receiving his words and deeds with acceptance, he should be eager to understand their secrets. For the imitator performs an act only because the Lawgiver (peace and blessings be upon him) performed it, and his act must have a secret in it, so he should search intensely into the secrets of deeds and words. For if he is content with memorising what is said, he is a vessel of knowledge and is not a scholar.
And therefore it used to be said, "So-and-so is among the vessels of knowledge"; he is not called a scholar if his concern is memorisation without insight into the wisdom and the secrets.
And whoever has had the covering lifted from his heart and has been illuminated by the light of guidance has become, in himself, one followed and imitated, so he should not imitate another.

And therefore Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) said, "There is no one whose knowledge is not taken up and left, except the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) (١)." He had learned jurisprudence from Zayd ibn Thabit and recited under Ubayy ibn Ka'b, then he differed from both of them in jurisprudence
and in recitation alike

And some of the early generations (salaf) said, "What comes to us from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) we accept with the fullest respect and obedience; what comes to us from the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) we take from and leave; and what comes to us from the Followers (tabi'un), they are men and we are men." The Companions' excellence lies only in their having witnessed the circumstantial indications of the states of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) and in their hearts being attached to matters grasped through those indications, which guided them to what is right in a way that does not come under transmission and wording, since there overflowed upon them from the light of prophethood what protected them, for the most part, from error.
And if reliance on what is heard from another is a disapproved imitation, then reliance on books and compilations is further still.

Indeed, books and compilations are newly arisen; none of them existed in the time of the Companions and the first Followers. They arose only after the year one hundred and twenty of the Hijra, after the death of all the Companions and the bulk of the Followers (may Allah be pleased with them), and after the death of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, and the best of the Followers. Indeed, the earlier ones disliked books of hadith and the compilation of books, lest people be occupied with them away from memorisation, from the Qur'an, and from reflection and remembrance. And they said, "Memorise as we used to memorise."

And therefore Abu Bakr and a group of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) disliked committing the Qur'an to writing in a written copy (mushaf), and they said, "How can we do something the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) did not do?" They feared people's reliance on written copies, and they said, "We leave the Qur'an to be received by some of them from others through dictation and recitation, so that this be their occupation and concern." This continued until Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) and the rest of the Companions pointed toward writing the Qur'an, for fear of people's neglect and laziness, and out of caution lest a dispute occur and there be found no source to refer back to concerning a word or a reading among those that resemble one another. Then Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was set at ease about this, and he gathered the Qur'an in one written copy.

And Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to object to Malik for compiling the Muwatta', saying, "He has innovated what the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) did not do." And it was said that the first book compiled in Islam was the book of Ibn Jurayj on reports (athar) and items of Qur'anic exegesis (tafsir) from Mujahid, Ata', and the companions of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) in Makkah.

Then the book of Ma'mar ibn Rashid as-San'ani in Yemen, in which he gathered transmitted Prophetic practices (sunan); then the book of the Muwatta' in Madinah by Malik ibn Anas; then the Jami' of Sufyan ath-Thawri.

Then in the fourth century, works of theology (kalam) appeared, and plunging into disputation and diving into the refutation of positions increased. Then people inclined to it, and to stories and preaching by means of them, so the knowledge of certainty began to fade from that time. After that, the knowledge of hearts, the examination of the traits of the self, and Satan's schemes came to be thought strange, and none but the fewest turned to it. So the disputant theologian came to be called a scholar, and the storyteller who embellishes his speech with rhymed expressions came to be called a scholar. This is because the common people are the ones who listen to them, so the reality of knowledge was not distinguished for them from what is not knowledge; and the way of life of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and their knowledge were not apparent among them, so that they might recognise by it how these people differ from them. So the name of scholars stuck to them, and the title was inherited by successors from predecessors, and the knowledge of the Hereafter became folded away, and the difference between knowledge and talk was lost to them, except to the elite among them, who, when it was said to them, "Is so-and-so more knowledgeable or so-and-so?" would say, "So-and-so has more knowledge and so-and-so has more talk."
So the elite used to perceive the difference between knowledge and the ability to talk.

Thus religion weakened in past centuries, so what do you suppose of this time of yours? Matters have reached the point that one who shows objection makes himself a target of being attributed to madness. So it is better that a person occupy himself with himself and keep silent.

And among them is that he be very cautious of newly invented matters, even if the majority agree on them; so the unanimity of people on what was invented after the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) must not deceive him. And let him be eager to investigate the states of the Companions, their way of life, their deeds, and what their greatest concern lay in: was it in teaching, compiling, debating, judging, governing, taking charge of endowments and bequests, consuming the property of orphans, mixing with sultans and being courteous to them in social dealings, or was it in fear, sorrow, reflection and spiritual struggle (mujahada), vigilance over the outward and the inward, avoiding sin small and great, and eagerness to perceive the hidden appetites of selves and the schemes of Satan, and the like

of the sciences of the inner. And know with certainty that the most knowledgeable of the people of the time and the closest of them to the truth are those most like the Companions and most acquainted with the way of the early generations (salaf), for from them religion was taken.

And therefore Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said, when it was said to him, "You have differed with so-and-so," "The best of us is the one who follows this religion most closely." So one should not be concerned about differing with the people of the age in agreeing with the people of the age of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him). For people formed an opinion regarding what they are engaged in because their natures incline to it, and their selves were not willing to admit that this is a cause of deprivation from Paradise, so they claimed that there is no way to Paradise other than it.
